fact: The Colorado Geological Survey calls expansive soil Colorado's most significant geologic hazard, with clays that can swell up to 20% by volume when wet.
quote: Innocuous as it sounds, Colorado's most significant geologic hazard is expansive or swelling soil — that is, soil laced with layers of various clays. … They can expand up to 20% by volume when exposed to water and exert a force of up to 30,000 pounds-per-square-foot, more than enough to break up any structure they encounter.
source_label: Colorado Geological Survey, Expansive Soil & Rock
notes: The same page elsewhere cites 10 percent / 20,000 psf in an older passage — quote the sentence above only.

fact: The Colorado Geological Survey lists poor surface drainage and planting next to foundations, so irrigation water soaks into the soil, among the landscaping problems on expansive soils.
quote: Improper landscaping problems include inadequate management of surface drainage and planting vegetation next to the foundation so irrigation water enters the soil.
source_label: Colorado Geological Survey, Expansive Soil & Rock
notes: Supports base-prep and drainage guidance. Never claim turf fixes foundation or subsidence problems.

fact: NRCS rates the Nunn and Weld soil series, common around the Larimer foothill towns, Longmont and Frederick–Dacono, as limited for building because of shrink-swell, while the sandy Olney, Otero, Vona and Kim soils are not flagged for it.
quote: ENG - Dwellings W/O Basements, survey areas CO644, CO617, CO618 and CO643: Nunn — "Somewhat limited" / "Very limited", reason "Shrink-swell" (18 components); Weld — "Somewhat limited", reason "Shrink-swell" (11 components); Olney, Vona — "Not limited"; Otero, Kim — limitations only for slope.
source_label: USDA-NRCS Soil Data Access (SSURGO) interpretation "ENG - Dwellings W/O Basements"
notes: Queried 2026-09-24. The interpretation is for small buildings, used here only as the shrink-swell signal NRCS publishes.

fact: The City of Longmont tells residents its clay soils absorb water slowly, so heavy watering runs off instead of soaking in.
quote: Longmont's clay soils absorb water slowly. If you water too much at once, the water runs off instead of soaking into the ground.
source_label: City of Longmont, Conserving Water Outdoors

fact: Greeley's water department says soils in the area tend to be shallow, with a layer of hard clay sometimes just inches below the surface.
quote: Our soils in this area tend to be shallow with a layer of hard clay, sometimes just inches below the surface.
source_label: City of Greeley Water & Sewer, Waterwise Landscapes
notes: Sits beside the sandy-loam SSURGO sample for central Greeley (nrcs-soil-greeley) — both can be true (sandy topsoil over calcareous clay subsoil).

fact: Soil surveys around central Fort Collins map mostly Fort Collins loam and Nunn clay loam, with high shrink-swell Nunn clay loam covering about 17% of the area sampled.
quote: SSURGO map units intersecting a ±0.02° box around central Fort Collins (share of box · max-horizon linear extensibility %): Fort Collins loam 0–3% slopes 25.3% (LEP 5.0) · Nunn clay loam 0–1% 16.5% (LEP 6.8) · Satanta loam 13.0% (LEP 3.8) · Altvan-Satanta loams 10.3% (LEP 4.5)
source_label: USDA-NRCS Soil Data Access (SSURGO), area-weighted query around central Fort Collins
notes: Queried 2026-09-24 (box ≈ 4.4 × 3.4 km around a town-center point; methodology choice, not an NRCS statement). Linear extensibility (LEP) ≥ 6 is high shrink-swell; ≈1.5 is low. Soils vary lot to lot — present as "soil surveys map…", never as a site finding.

notes: Queried 2026-09-30: 9 x 9 point grid over ±0.02° around the Census internal point (40.367046, -105.533861), SDA_Get_Mukey_from_intersection_with_WktWgs84 per point, muaggatt.brockdepmin (cm).
